cues.text: A Convert and Married Bishop
Born around 310 into a pagan noble family at Poitiers , in Roman Gaul, Hilary converted to Christianity as an adult through his own philosophical searching.
He was already married, with a daughter, Abra, when chosen bishop of his native city around 353.
This promotion was common enough for married men in that era, provided they thereafter lived in continence.
Confronting Arianism in Gaul
Arianism, though largely a controversy of the Greek East, had begun creeping into Gaul through the influence of bishops like Saturninus of Arles.
Hilary, exposing Saturninus's heterodoxy, convened a council to confront him at Béziers in 356, but the Arian-dominated assembly refused even to hear him.
Exile to Phrygia
Denounced to the pro-Arian Emperor Constantius II soon after, Hilary was banished to Phrygia in Asia Minor, far from his own diocese.
Rather than let exile silence him, he used the years abroad productively, mastering Greek theological sources unfamiliar to most Latin churchmen.

He composed major works, including the beginnings of his monumental treatise On the Trinity , earning him, by tradition, the title 'Athanasius of the West' for his tireless defense of Nicene doctrine.
Return and Continued Struggle
So effective and disruptive was Hilary's advocacy even in exile that Arian bishops in the East, alarmed by his influence, persuaded Constantius to send the troublesome Gallic bishop back home in 360.

Hilary returned to Poitiers in triumph in 361, welcomed by his own flock, and continued his campaign against Arianism, notably challenging the Arian bishop Auxentius of Milan at a synod in 364; although Hilary denounced him, Auxentius retained his see.
Teacher of St. Martin
During these years Hilary became mentor to a young soldier-turned-monk named Martin , later bishop of Tours.
He encouraged Martin to found a monastery at Ligugé near Poitiers around 360, among the earliest monastic foundations in Gaul.
It formed a link between Hilary's theological rigor and the growth of Western monasticism.
Legacy
Hilary died at Poitiers around 368, having spent his episcopate defending, in the words later applied to him, the divinity of Christ against an empire and much of its episcopate tilted toward heresy.
Declared a Doctor of the Church in 1851, he is remembered as one of the first great Latin theologians to master and transmit the deep Trinitarian reflection of the Greek East to the Christian West.
